<reason>Both sides built coherent, well-structured cases—PRO on rent extraction and the availability of substitute enforcement mechanisms, CON on the speed and scale advantages of integrated platform control for protecting vulnerable users. The pivotal clash was whether "baseline security standards" (certificate revocation, chargebacks, licensing) can truly replicate the platform's unilateral kill-switch. CON pressed this repeatedly and effectively, forcing PRO into conceding in closing that competition-based enforcement is merely "slower," a concession that matters precisely because CON's whole case is that speed is what prevents irreversible harm (stolen identities, drained accounts) to kids and elderly users. CON's answers to pressure questions (offshore processors evading licensing, defaults eroding once giants have financial incentive to steer users) were more concretely tied to mechanism than PRO's assurances that baseline rules would simply "exclude" such loopholes. PRO's economic/rent-extraction framing remained strong and mostly unanswered on the merits, but CON explicitly absorbed it into a safety-tradeoff frame ("seatbelt that sometimes fails") rather than ignoring it. On balance CON did slightly more to defend the security half of the motion's own qualifier ("under baseline security standards"), giving it a clear but not dominant edge.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's Turn 8 answer to Q2 ("A paper refund rule is not a kill switch... law moves in months, banks in weeks, phishing in minutes") most damaged PRO's live route, because PRO's closing could only concede the speed gap as a "tuning problem" rather than refute it.</best_rebuttal>
